items_missed: No 'sound good?' confirmation on the agenda. Let me run through these details real quick and then we'll get that scheduled for you' — but it ended as a statement, not a check. The customer's 'Okay. Okay.' was volunteered, not asked for, which is why the differentiator flag does not fire.
Never asked 'how are you today?' The customer opened with 'Hey, good morning' and got 'Oh, okay. Let me reach out to her and see if I can get you transferred over to her real quick.'

The move date was never established. Not the target date, not a window, not even 'when are you looking to move.' A 2200 sqft interstate-adjacent household move was scoped, routed to a walkthrough, and closed out without anyone knowing when it happens — which also means availability was never checked and the walkthrough has no deadline attached to it.

Additional rooms never asked. No garage, no attic, no shed, no storage unit probe on a 2200 sqft single-story house — and the customer's own special-considerations answer was almost entirely garage contents ('a 72 inch toolbox and then a weight system and then a treadmill'), which should have prompted the follow-up and did not.
Packing needs never asked. On a three-bedroom-plus-office house, whether they want packing service is a major scope and revenue question and it was never put.
Box count never asked.
Storage stops never asked.
Additional stops never asked.

Moving stressors never asked — no 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?' On a customer who had already missed one scheduled call and volunteered 'we'll be moving [the antiques] ourselves,' there was an opening to find out why.

Entire pricing section absent — 4/20, and all four points are automatic N/A grants on trip fee and packing pricing. No hourly rate, no per-mover framing, no what's-included list, no No Worries Damage Coverage, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee, no 'no hidden fees.' On a walkthrough-scheduler the specific quote is legitimately deferred — the differentiators are not. This customer hung up knowing nothing about why Einstein is different from the next mover he calls, and he has at least a day before anyone speaks to him again.
Entire clock section absent — 0/4. No start trigger, no 2.5 hour minimum, no fifteen-minute proration, no sense-check.

Drive time never mentioned. New Braunfels to La Vernia is roughly forty-five minutes each way from a San Antonio base — a material line item on the eventual estimate and a trip-fee question — and it never came up even as a heads-up.
Disassembly and reassembly never raised, on a four-bedroom destination.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. No prep-equals-shorter-move framing, no consolidation examples, no carload tip. A prep speech on a walkthrough-scheduler is arguably worth more than on a normal call, not less: the customer has days before the walkthrough and would arrive at it with a smaller, tidier inventory.

The walkthrough was never actually booked. This is the core miss. The customer offered his own availability twice and unprompted — 'we could do that tomorrow or this evening fits you guys with' and then 'Tomorrow tomorrow would be better anytime tomorrow we can make work' and finally 'It doesn't matter. Whatever's easiest for you guys' — and the call ended with 'I'll let her know tomorrow kind of anytime and she'll either give you a call or shoot you a text to get that set up.' A customer with zero constraints was handed back to a queue instead of put on a calendar.
No deposit required never mentioned.

No email at all. No confirmation of the walkthrough, no email address captured or read back, no written record that anything was agreed. The only artifact of this five-minute call is a note Dustin says he will pass to Amy.
BOLDED key details and 'reply with any corrections' never mentioned.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' The call closed on 'well we definitely appreciate you and I hope you have a great rest of your day.'
Customer's name used zero times after capturing it. He asked 'What's a good first and last name for you?', got 'James, Berumen B-E-R-U-M-E-N,' and never said it again.
top_strength: Dustin's best moment is the one the rubric does not have a box for: he explained the virtual walkthrough from scratch, patiently, the instant the customer revealed he did not know what it was. 'What you guys come to us or we just did it or I don't know what their virtual walkthrough is but' got 'No problem. Sorry about that. So it's essentially kinda like video call, we would send you a link you click in and then you'd walk through the home. We'd be frantically taking notes of everything getting an idea of everything you're moving, and then we'd compare those notes from what we typically would see from a home of your size and then get your estimate built up and then emailed over to you and then chat with you about the details of your estimate and get you onto the schedule.' That is the whole downstream process in one breath, it apologizes for the jargon rather than the customer's question, and it ends by naming the outcome the customer actually wants. The customer's reply — 'Okay, we could do that tomorrow or this evening' — shows it converted an unknown into a yes. The routing decision itself was also correct and correctly framed. He recognized 2200 sqft as walkthrough territory immediately and gave the customer the reason before the ask: 'being the size of your house we generally I can run through and get the information and then we would get a virtual walkthrough set up with you so that way we can tailor your estimate to move.' Sending a 2200 sqft home to a walkthrough rather than guessing at it is exactly the behavior that moves the estimate-accuracy number, and he did it without hesitation. His special-considerations probe was well-built too — 'do you have any special considerations for your move? These are usually heavier things like safe and pianos or delicate things like antique or glass or marble furniture' gives the customer categories instead of an abstraction, and it surfaced the toolbox, the cable pulley weight system and the treadmill. He then followed up on the one that needed it: 'that weight system is that like a cable pulley system.' And he confirmed access at both ends in plain language, getting '25 to 27 feet' at the origin and 'you can park right next to the garage. So it's like ten feet' at the destination. Five minutes, no wasted words, no confusion.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is worth more than everything else on this call combined: book the walkthrough on the call. James gave Dustin an open calendar three separate times and said 'whatever's easiest for you guys,' and the call ended with a promise that a third person would reach out sometime tomorrow. That is a warm, flexible, ready-to-schedule customer converted into a callback task. The line needed was: 'Perfect — let's just put it on the calendar right now so it doesn't slip. Amy has tomorrow at ten or tomorrow at two. Which works better?' Then confirm the email and send it: 'I'll send you a confirmation for that right now — you'll get the link in it, and if anything in there looks off just reply and let me know.' That single change turns a 2/11 booking section into something respectable and, more importantly, it is the difference between a walkthrough that happens and one that gets chased. Second priority: this call has no date on it. A 2200 sqft three-bedroom-plus-office household move was fully scoped without anyone asking when it is happening. Everything downstream — availability, crew sizing, whether the walkthrough is urgent or leisurely, whether this is even a viable lead — depends on that one question. Put it in the first thirty seconds, permanently. Third, the differentiators are not optional on a walkthrough-scheduler. Pricing scored 4/20 and every point was automatic. The specific dollar quote is properly deferred to the walkthrough, but 'no deposit to hold a date,' 'up to $2,000 No Worries Damage Coverage on every move,' 'you'll get an email with your mover's photo before the day,' and 'if we miss your arrival window we start discounting immediately' cost about twenty seconds and are the entire reason a customer waits for Einstein's estimate instead of taking whoever quotes first. James is going to talk to other movers between now and tomorrow, and right now he has nothing to compare them against. Fourth, use the name. He asked for it, got it, and never said it once — and closed with 'we definitely appreciate you' where 'we definitely appreciate you, James' costs nothing. Estimate-accuracy note: no quote was given, which on a 2200 sqft home is the correct call and should be recognized as such — routing to a walkthrough instead of guessing is the behavior the 46%-to-80% push actually needs. The one gap worth flagging for the walkthrough handoff is that New Braunfels to La Vernia is roughly a forty-five minute haul each way and drive time was never mentioned to the customer or, apparently, noted for Amy. If that lands as a surprise on the estimate email it will read as a hidden fee, which is the opposite of the brand promise.
phone_presence_notes: Courteous, clear and easy to deal with, with one genuinely gracious recovery — 'No problem. Sorry about that' when the customer did not know what a virtual walkthrough was — but the warmth is procedural rather than personal: 'Gotcha' six times as the entire acknowledgment vocabulary, the customer's name captured and then never used once, no humor, no empathy marker, and no question about the customer beyond the inventory.
audio_review_reason: Short call (5.8 minutes) with a compliant, low-affect customer whose longest reply is eleven words, which leaves thin evidence either way — the score sits right on the 2/3 boundary and the difference between 'efficient and pleasant' and 'clipped and processing a ticket' is entirely in the delivery, which this transcript cannot show. Audio is also needed to confirm that the repeated 'Gotcha' reads as engaged acknowledgment rather than a verbal tic that cuts the customer off.
